extracted.intended_audience: journalists, news organizations, media researchers, policymakers, and the interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate attributes that make news organizations more or less trustworthy, based on a Gallup/Knight Foundation national survey and conjoint experiment. Useful for journalists and news organizations seeking to understand drivers of public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A news organization's overall commitment to accuracy in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated the single most important factor (89% say commitment to accuracy is very important). Conjoint analysis shows accuracy factors explain about half the variability in choices between hypothetical news sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quickly and openly correcting mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly and visibly an organization corrects errors and whether corrections are made openly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 86% rate this as very important. Conjoint results: compared with quick and visible corrections, respondents were 28 percentage points less likely to choose a source that rarely reports corrections, 18 points less likely if corrections are occasional, and 8 points less likely if corrections are quick but not highly visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful evaluation of facts before reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: How carefully an organization checks and evaluates facts before publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a core accuracy attribute in the conjoint task and among top drivers of perceived trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record of having published inaccurate or false information
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization's history of publishing inaccurate or false stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 77% say this record is very important in determining trust; a negative record reduces perceived trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency with which organizations make mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: How often a news organization makes factual or reporting mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 53% rate frequency of mistakes as very important to trust judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: A demonstrated commitment to fair, unbiased or nonpartisan reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 78% say commitment to fairness is very important; many respondents mention fair or unbiased reporting as a reason to trust an outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived bias (biased, slanted, or unfair reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reporting is perceived as one-sided, slanted, or politically biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dominant cause of distrust: 42% spontaneously cited biased/slanted reporting and three-quarters mentioned bias-related reasons at least once when explaining distrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing fact-checking resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the organization provides explicit fact-checking resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 74% rate providing fact-checking resources as very important to trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization’s openness about reporting practices, sources, and potential conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 71% rate commitment to transparency as very important. Conjoint analysis finds transparency (disclosing conflicts, making extra materials available) accounts for ~27% of decisions after accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing links to research and facts to back up reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether stories include links or references to research, data, and verifiable facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 71% say this is very important; especially valued by younger adults (83% of 18–34 vs. 65% of older adults).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly distinguishing news from commentary/analysis/advertiser-paid content
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the outlet makes a clear separation between factual news reporting and opinion, analysis, or sponsored content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 64% rate this as very important to their trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception that the organization is neutral (not holding or promoting a partisan stance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 58% say neutrality is very important, though this resonates less with Democrats (44%) than independents (64%) and Republicans (68%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters sharing their political views
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reporters publicly share their own political views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only 5% of respondents say it is very important that reporters share their political views (low importance factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlet giving positive coverage to groups/issues the respondent agrees with
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the outlet gives favorable coverage to people, groups, or issues that align with the respondent's own views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 10% rate this as very important, indicating it is not a major driver of trust overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cues or endorsements from political leaders, family, or friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether endorsements or cues from leaders or personal networks influence trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally low importance: endorsements from political leaders (8% very important) and family/friends (5% very important).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of issues covered
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific topics and issues that an outlet focuses its coverage on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 43% regard the types of issues covered as very important to their trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters understand challenges 'people like me' face
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reporters demonstrate understanding of the problems and experiences of people like the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 32% rate this as very important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of awards the organization has won
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether accolades and awards for reporting influence trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the least important factors: only 4% say number of awards is very important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size: circulation or viewership
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization’s audience size or reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also among the least important: 4% say circulation/viewership is very important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local versus national coverage (location of the source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the outlet is local or national and whether the source is U.S.-based or abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low importance overall (local 5% very important, national 8% very important), but matters slightly more to older adults and Republicans.

rubrics_metrics.name: History, longevity, or reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: How long the news organization has been reporting and its historical reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 10% say longevity is very important; more frequently cited by college graduates (14%) than nongraduates (5%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Who owns the news organization and whether ownership raises concerns about conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a dimension in the conjoint task but accounted for a relatively small share of respondents' preferences compared with accuracy, transparency, and partisan reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making additional reporting material publicly available
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing extra materials (e.g., full unedited interviews, source documents) beyond stories themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjoint: making additional reporting material publicly available increased the chance a respondent would choose a source by about 9 percentage points compared with not making such material available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosing potential conflicts of interest (sponsors and owners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the organization acknowledges conflicts of interest about sponsors, owners, and other potential influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjoint: respondents were somewhat less likely to choose organizations that 'usually' rather than 'always' acknowledged conflicts, and substantially less likely to favor organizations that generally do not acknowledge conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan reputation / perceived partisan leaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A news organization’s reputation for favoring Democratic, Republican, or mixed/unclear partisan positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partisan reputations reduce trust among partisans when the reputation opposes their own views (Republicans 22 percentage points less likely to choose Democratic-leaning sources; Democrats 12 points less likely to choose Republican-leaning). Partisans were not more likely to choose sources with a sympathetic partisan reputation than ones with mixed/unclear reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy vs. speed tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the outlet prioritizes speed of reporting over accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjoint: prioritizing speed over accuracy reduced likelihood of being chosen as more trustworthy by about 19 percentage points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing, completeness, and citation of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether stories include complete details, cite sources, and rely on reliable/credible sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Younger adults are more likely to cite completeness, details and cited sources as reasons to trust (17% of 18–34) compared with older adults (6%); similarly for citing 'reliable or credible sources' (11% younger vs. 4% older).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credible, honest, ethical or reputable reporting (journalistic ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adherence to journalistic ethics and a reputation for credibility and honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 31% of respondents mention credible, honest, ethical or reputable reporting as a reason they trust an organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good or professional journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived quality and professionalism of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 18% mention good or professional journalism as a trust-building factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand awareness and respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarity with and respect for the outlet’s brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importance varies by subgroup: more important to Democrats (49%) and Republicans (39%) than to independents (25%), and more important to highly attentive news consumers (47%) than less attentive (27%).
